newsitem.title: USA: Keep tobacco stocks, Florida pension staff urges.
newsitem.headline: Keep tobacco stocks, Florida pension staff urges.

text.p: Florida should keep the tobacco stocks it holds in its $60 billion pension fund because the stocks are making money, state staffers and outside advisers said in a report to Gov. Lawton Chiles and other officials who oversee the fund.

Tom Herndon, the newly appointed executive director of the Board of Administration, summed up the report's message as, "At the present time that (tobacco) is still a fairly good investment that is generating a pretty good return."
Florida's tobacco holdings include Philip Morris Cos Inc and RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp.
In a telephone interview Tuesday, Herndon said return on investment should be the "first and foremost criteria" in deciding whether to keep the tobacco stocks.
"(Are) the state board and the pensioners benefitting from having tobacco stocks in its overall portfolio? My general impression is that they are," Herndon said.
Florida is among the states that have sued the tobacco companies to recoup tax money spent treating smoking-related illnesses.
The fund, which covers 600,000 current state, county, city and school employees and 153,000 retirees, holds about $693 million of tobacco stocks, or about 1.3 percent of its total.
The fund's Board of Administration -- Chiles, Florida Comptroller Bob Milligan and Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson -- are to decide in December whether the state should divest its tobacco stocks.

In its 65-page report, the board of administration staff said that over 10 years, the tobacco stocks listed in the Wilshire 2500 index saw a 23 percent return, while non-tobacco stocks in the index returned 14.2 percent.
"We believe the divestiture from the portfolio of all tobacco issues would negatively impact future performance," one of the the fund's outside managers wrote in the report.

Another of its outside manager suggested the state could be sued if it divests tobacco stocks from the pension fund, on grounds that it was making investment decisions based on "non-economic considerations."
The report cautioned that barring tobacco stocks could lead to the adoption of additional "social objectives," further limiting diversification and reducing returns.
It examined equity funds that prohibited investment in companies involved with socially controversial products and services such as alcohol, tobacco, gambling, abortion, apartheid and nuclear energy.

"For the one-, three- and five-year periods, the funds with multiple constraints underperformed the broader indices by 5 to 6 percentage points," the report said. "This magnitude of underperformance, if applied to the size of our current equity portfolio, would be $1.4 billion a year."
Herndon said Florida's pension fund has outperformed the Standard & Poor's 500 index, and exceeded actuarial requirements over the past several years. He said he plans no major changes.

"My very strong impression is the pension fund has a very admirable track record," he said. "There's nothing that I intend to do that is dramatic in the sense of a change of direction. I hope to be able to continue in the path of my predecessor."

Herndon, 50, replaces executive director Ash Williams Jr, who resigned to join a private investment firm. He was formerly Chiles' chief of staff and most recently was executive director of the Florida Department of Revenue.
